summary.en: At the end of the psychedelic wave, hippie culture moved from underground into the mainstream and deeply shaped mainstream culture after 1969.
summary.zh: 在迷幻风潮的末期，嬉皮文化逐渐从地下成为了主流，并对1969年后的主流文化产生了深远影响。

body.zh:
在迷幻风潮的末期，嬉皮文化逐渐从地下成为了主流，并对1969年后的主流文化产生了深远影响。

在1967年的夏天，迷幻成为了音乐市场的主流。我们可以用几分钟时间审视一下，迷幻是如何从伦敦和旧金山的亚文化中蔓延开来的。它也在洛杉矶、东海岸的纽约北部形成了一定影响。我们主要想研究它如何从一种名不见经传的音乐形式，摇身一变走进了千家万户，成为了一种全国青年普遍的生活方式、文化等等方面的代表。

我们首先谈谈音乐节，尤其是那些能吸引大量人群的音乐节。第一个重要的嬉皮摇滚音乐节可能是1967年6月的蒙特利尔国际流行音乐节，它由The Mamas and The Papas的成员John Phillips和制作人Lou Adler联合举办。他们邀请到了许多嘉宾乐队。最重要的是，在某些方面这场音乐节成就了Jimi Hendrix，因为这是他在全国范围内最具突破性的表演之一。音乐节还邀请到了The Jefferson Airplane、Grateful Dead、The Who、Janis Joplin、The Byrds、The Mamas and the Papas和The Animals这样的乐队，而The Beach Boys推掉了这次演出。甚至连Otis Redding也参与了这次演出——乐队吉他手Steve Cropper常常谈到 他们在带着他们的小吉他音箱，穿着马海毛西服，为台下那些衣着五颜六色、坐拥巨大Marshall音箱的嬉皮士表演时是多么胆战心惊——但是人们普遍认为正是这场演出使得Otis Redding名声大噪。

在1967年6月到1969年8月的伍德斯托克音乐节这段时间，这类音乐节迅速蔓延全国。诸如亚特兰大音乐节这样的盛会都是以其为基础创办的。我们发现，这些能召集大量人群的大规模国际摇滚音乐节引领着嬉皮音乐和文化的发展。如果蒙特利尔音乐节是作为开始而存在，那么1969年夏天的伍德斯托克音乐节则是嬉皮士运动的尾声。这场名垂青史的室外摇滚音乐节主要靠一个名叫Michael Lang的人举办。伍德斯托克的嘉宾名单与蒙特利尔音乐节有不少重叠，但除此以外Santana，Crosby、Stills & Nash在此次音乐节上迎来了首次亮相，参加音乐节演出的同时还有Joe Cocker、Sly and the Family Stone。这场音乐节以几乎没有引来麻烦而闻名。试想一下：把这么多人塞到一场音乐节里面，想想那些可能出现的差错；这类音乐节自然还会产生很多其他麻烦：例如有人吸毒过量或者打架斗殴之类的事情发生，但在一场曲棍球比赛里你也可以看到同样的事情，只不过不是吸毒过量，而是饮酒过量罢了。总而言之，这些事故并没有那么不同寻常。

然而在1969年底，一些不美好的事发生了，给嬉皮年代划下了一个并不完美的句点，那就是1969年12月举办的阿尔塔蒙德高速公路免费音乐节 (Altamont Speedway Free Festival) 。一直以来，办一场免费的室外音乐节是The Rolling Stones的夙愿，但他们在寻找合适场地的过程中却屡屡碰壁。最终，他们选定了旧金山市外不远处的阿尔塔蒙德高速公路。曾经成功举办伍德斯托克音乐节的Michael Lang也协助了此次音乐节的组织工作。 The Rolling Stones成功上了头条，他们打算拍一部叫做《Gimme Shelter》的电影，并在不久后的1970年上映。

为了拍摄到理想的打光镜头，他们一直等到太阳落山。但不幸的是，他们决定动用地狱天使 (Hells Angels) 负责本场音乐节的安保工作——至少参加那场演出工作的那些地狱天使并非是现场保安的最好选择。最后事态失控，有人直接在舞台前被杀，这一幕被镜头捕捉，能清楚看见是在Mick Jagger正前方。这是一场真正的悲剧，也是嬉皮运动中一个真正的污点，许多成功的音乐节因阿尔塔蒙德而消失了。但我认为我们讨论音乐节的重要之处是去思考，当这些音乐节在全国各大城市生根发芽时，你才能真正感受到嬉皮文化中年轻人混在一起的感觉。这是一股席卷全国的热潮，它开始变得主流化了，不仅发生在伦敦或旧金山，在英国其他地方也有类似的音乐节，比如Isle of White音乐节就值得我们回味。与此同时，音乐开始通过调频广播播放。一开始这只是调频音乐电台众多创始人之一Tom Donahue在1967年的一个无心之举，从此以后音乐开始通过这种渠道蔓延全国，以至于后来几乎每个大城市都有一到两个调频摇滚电台，人们必须确保人手一个调频收音机，以保证人人都能在车上收到调频信号。转眼间，收音机所到之处，音乐就得以传播，这带给了音乐作品相当可观的曝光率。调幅广播曾经被the Beach Boys、Beatles和the Byrds的歌曲所统治，现在它成为了一些廉价流行歌曲的传播平台，几乎已经低龄化到了青少年歌曲的程度。调频电台逐渐向摇滚风格和传统摇滚靠拢。当我们回顾1967、1968和1969年间调幅广播和调频广播的发展时，至少是我们在这堂课里谈到的摇滚乐，紧紧跟随着调频广播所传播的那些乐队的步伐，而调幅广播则变成了商业流行乐的平台。这些现象是导致嬉皮文化从一种迷幻亚文化，成功突破到主流市场的诱因。一开始，迷幻摇滚就是伦敦和旧金山迷幻亚文化中叛逆风潮的代表，只是在之后，由于国家性的曝光以及音乐的普及等因素促使了它的日常化，以至于1969到1970年间印第安纳波利斯的一个孩子都可以走进商场，买到一件和旧金山嬉皮士一样的扎染衬衫，哪怕他对这种迷幻亚文化的发展毫无体验。这只是嬉皮文化从迷幻亚文化转变为主流流行文化时众多事件中的一个例子。1969年末 1970年初通常被认为是一个转折点。我们将在摇滚史第二部分中继续讲述这段故事。曾经在1960年互相融合的众多音乐形式，将会在我们迈入70年代时分离成专门的风格流派。如果你还记得Pink Floyd的专辑《Dark Side of the Moon》的封面——也就是那幅白光射入三棱镜而折射出不同色彩的图片，那束白光好比迷幻音乐，而什么将会从中折射出来呢？是这些形形色色的流派：前卫摇滚、乡村摇滚、唱作歌手、布鲁斯摇滚，它们全部来源于迷幻音乐，而这就是摇滚史第二部分中故事的大致方向。当我们回顾迷幻时代时，我们总会谈到迷幻亚文化，主流文化，毒品及对幻觉的渴望。音乐的迷幻化，以及音乐和音乐人如何借力于此而变得越来越雄心勃勃，他们开始关心音乐是否能流传后世，而并非仅仅把音乐当做一种销售专辑的临时手段。这种野心，这种迷幻年代的观念性本质，开始真正地定义70年代以及之后的音乐，特别是流行乐。

我们第一部分的课程已经接近尾声，希望能在摇滚史第二部分中再次见到你们。
body.en:
At the end of the psychedelic wave, hippie culture moved from underground into the mainstream and deeply shaped mainstream culture after 1969.

In summer 1967 psychedelia became mainstream in the music market. We can take a few minutes to see how it spread from London and San Francisco subcultures. It also had some impact in Los Angeles and upstate New York on the East Coast. We want to study how a little-known music form walked into ordinary homes and became a lifestyle and cultural marker for young people nationwide.

First, festivals—especially those that drew huge crowds. The first major hippie rock festival may have been the Monterey International Pop Festival in June 1967, co-organized by John Phillips of the Mamas and the Papas and producer Lou Adler. They booked many guest bands. Most important, in some ways the festival made Jimi Hendrix—one of his most breakthrough national performances. Also Jefferson Airplane, the Grateful Dead, the Who, Janis Joplin, the Byrds, the Mamas and the Papas, the Animals; the Beach Boys turned it down. Even Otis Redding played—guitarist Steve Cropper often talks about how nervous they were arriving with small guitar amps in mohair suits while colorful hippies sat before huge Marshall stacks—but people generally say that show made Otis Redding’s name.

From June 1967 to Woodstock in August 1969 such festivals spread fast nationwide. Events like the Atlanta festival were built on that model. We find that large international rock festivals that gathered masses led the growth of hippie music and culture. If Monterey was the start, summer 1969’s Woodstock was the end of the hippie movement. That historic outdoor rock festival was mainly put on by Michael Lang. Woodstock’s guest list overlapped Monterey, but Santana and Crosby, Stills & Nash also debuted there, with Joe Cocker and Sly and the Family Stone. The festival was famous for almost no trouble. Imagine packing that many people in; think of what could go wrong. Such festivals naturally bring other problems—overdoses, fights—but you see the same at a hockey game, only drinking instead of overdosing. In short, those incidents were not that unusual.

Yet at the end of 1969 something ugly happened that closed the hippie years imperfectly: the Altamont Speedway Free Festival in December 1969. A free outdoor festival had long been a Rolling Stones wish, but they kept hitting walls finding a site. Finally they chose Altamont Speedway not far outside San Francisco. Michael Lang, who had run Woodstock, also helped organize. The Stones made headlines; they planned a film, Gimme Shelter, released in 1970.

To get the lighting they wanted they waited until sunset. Unfortunately they used Hells Angels for security—at least those Angels at that show were not the best choice for crowd control. Things got out of hand; someone was killed right in front of the stage, caught on camera clearly in front of Mick Jagger. A real tragedy and a real stain on the hippie movement; many successful festivals vanished after Altamont. But the important point about festivals is: when they took root in major cities nationwide, you could really feel young people mixing in hippie culture. It became a national wave and went mainstream—not only London or San Francisco; Britain had similar festivals, such as the Isle of Wight, worth remembering. At the same time music spread via FM. At first it was almost an accident of one FM founder, Tom Donahue, in 1967; then it spread nationwide until almost every big city had one or two FM rock stations, and people needed FM radios so cars could pick up the signal. Wherever radio went, music followed—considerable exposure. AM, once ruled by Beach Boys, Beatles, and Byrds songs, became a platform for cheap pop, almost teen-song level. FM moved toward rock and classic rock. Looking back at AM and FM in 1967–69, at least for the rock we discuss in this course, it followed the bands FM carried, while AM became commercial pop. Those shifts helped hippie culture break from psychedelic subculture into the mainstream market. At first psychedelic rock stood for the rebellious wave in London and San Francisco subcultures; later national exposure and musical spread made it everyday—so that by 1969–70 a kid in Indianapolis could walk into a mall and buy a tie-dye shirt like a San Francisco hippie’s, even with no experience of that subculture’s growth. One example among many of hippie culture moving from psychedelic subculture into mainstream pop culture. Late 1969 / early 1970 is usually seen as a turning point. We continue that story in Part Two of History of Rock. Musical forms that had fused in the 1960s would split into specialized styles as we enter the 1970s. If you remember the cover of Pink Floyd’s The Dark Side of the Moon—white light entering a prism and splitting into colors—that white light is like psychedelic music; what refracts out? Progressive rock, country rock, singer-songwriters, blues rock—all from psychedelia; that is roughly Part Two’s direction. Looking back at the psychedelic era we always talk subculture, mainstream, drugs, and the hunger for hallucination. The psychedelicizing of music, and how music and musicians used it to grow more ambitious—caring whether music would last, not only as a temporary means to sell albums. That ambition, that conceptual essence of the psychedelic years, began truly to define the 1970s and after—especially popular music.

Part One of the course is nearly over; we hope to see you again in Part Two of History of Rock.
